title: Forget Ice Trays: These Machines Make Chewable Nugget Ice
summary:
If you love chewing ice but hate the hard, jagged cubes from your freezer, nugget ice might be your new best friend. Also known as pellet ice or "Sonic ice," it's made of compacted flakes that are soft, airy, and easy to munch. It's slow to melt, so it keeps drinks cold without watering them down. And it soaks up flavor, making it great for sodas, iced coffee, or just water.

Nugget ice makers are becoming popular home appliances, but they're more complex than regular ice makers. They have more internal parts, so they cost more — often starting around $400. Popular Mechanics tested several models from brands like GE, Euhomy, and Gevi. They timed how long each machine took to make a batch of ice and fill its basket. They also checked ease of use and ice quality.

The GE Profile Opal 2.0 Ultra won their top pick. It's about the size of two shoeboxes side by side, and it can make enough ice for a big party. It has an app for scheduling maintenance and a sleek design. But it can be noisy when producing ice — about as loud as a loud refrigerator. The Euhomy Smart is smaller but powerful, making 40 pounds of ice per day. Its first batch is ready in under 10 minutes. The Gevi 2.0 has the largest bin, holding almost 5 pounds, and its door opens to 90 degrees for easy scooping. However, it takes a few hours to fill the basket completely.

These machines are great for entertaining or just upgrading your daily drinks. They might be pricey, but for ice lovers, they could be worth it. No more struggling with ice trays!
why_it_matters: How we judge a product — by price, noise, speed or capacity — shapes what companies build next, and this story shows that a restaurant technology moving into kitchens is judged by the same trade-offs students face when choosing between cheap, fast and good.

background_read: Nugget ice is not new: commercial machines were first built for restaurants and hospitals, where soft, chewable ice is easier to crunch and safer for patients. The American drive-in chain Sonic made it famous by serving it in every drink, which is why many people call it 'Sonic ice.'

Popular Mechanics is a long-running American magazine that tests and reviews machines and gadgets, so its timed tests give shoppers a way to compare products that look almost identical on a store page.

GE (General Electric) is a large American company that has made home appliances for more than a century, while Euhomy and Gevi are smaller brands that sell mostly online and compete on price and features.

The trend here is 'trickle-down' technology: ice machines that once filled restaurant bins are being shrunk into countertop boxes, but the extra parts — a compressor, a cutter and a press — keep prices far above a plastic ice tray.

perspectives.description: Nugget ice is soft to chew, melts slowly so drinks don't get watery, and a countertop machine means never running out at a party. The tested models all delivered good ice, just in different amounts and speeds.

Starting around $400, these machines cost far more than a tray or a regular ice maker, and the most expensive one can still be as loud as a refrigerator. More internal parts also means more things that can break.

The pattern is familiar: equipment built for restaurants becomes a home gadget, and independent testing becomes the map shoppers use. The 'best' machine depends entirely on the criteria — capacity, speed, noise or size.

As the category grows, competition will likely push prices down and add features like quieter compressors, app controls and bigger bins. The real test will be whether early buyers think the upgrade was worth the money.
